paragraphs.text: Should Parcelbird launch its own quick-commerce service in 2027?
Board discussion document, January 2027
Parcelbird
Board (two founders and two investors)
Synthetic benchmark data: company and figures are fictional

slides.title: Executive summary

paragraphs.text: Executive summary
Parcelbird should not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027 and should put the cash into scaling its software instead
Quick commerce is growing fast, but no operator has made it pay
–	US sales grew from $1.8B in 2022 to $5.1B in 2025, yet both incumbents lose money on every order
At the inputs Parcelbird's own customer sites achieve, every order loses money
–	A median-site order loses $6.17, and even the best observed inputs lose $1.76
–	The plan's profit needs every driver above the best site, a mix no site has reached
Customers stay less and cost more to win than the plan needs
–	22% of pop-up customers still ordered in month three; 44% of residents said weekly
–	Even on plan, a customer who stays takes about 28 months to repay their acquisition cost
The launch breaks the investors' runway floor even if everything goes to plan
–	Runway falls to about 6 months by month 18, half the 12-month floor
–	At median inputs, nine stores would lose about $18M a year
Scaling the software for grocers who want their own fast delivery is the better use of cash
–	The pipeline could add $3.6M of ARR for about $1.2M of new cash to month 18, against $9.5M for the launch
